section_summary: This section is dominated by May–June 1941 newspaper editorials, letters, cartoons, and reports protesting continued American petroleum exports to Japan while Harold L. Ickes warned of tanker shortages, gasoline restrictions, and “gasless Sundays” in the eastern United States. The clippings debate whether the shortage reflected inadequate transportation, diversion of American tankers to Britain, government policy, or oil-industry interests, and they describe Japanese ships loading petroleum at American ports. The final pages contain July–August State Department correspondence concerning Japanese bunkering in Brazil, Japanese inquiries about Bolivian rubber, Governor Culbert L. Olson’s demand for a complete embargo, and aviation gasoline storage at Dairen.

subfiles.title: Japanese tanker departure and cargo (fragment)
subfiles.about: Reports the departure of a tanker carrying oil and aviation gasoline with Japanese naval personnel aboard.
subfiles.summary: Fragment: a departing Japanese tanker carried two naval officers and thirteen navy men, with 62,000 barrels of oil and 18,000 of aviation gasoline from Associated Oil docks.

subfiles.title: Is It Necessary?
subfiles.about: Questions proposed American fuel restrictions while petroleum continues to be exported to Japan and Russia.
subfiles.summary: Editorial 'Is It Necessary?' accepts gasless Sundays only with genuine need and stronger authority than Ickes's assertion, and wants rationing to await an end to exports to Japan and Russia.

subfiles.title: Sunday driving, oil conservation, and exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Considers restrictions on Sunday driving and challenges continued petroleum shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Editorial suggests closing filling stations part of weekends, doubts Ickes's authority, and asks why West Coast gasoline and fuel oil still go to Japan if conservation is essential.

subfiles.title: Federal control of the oil industry
subfiles.about: Reviews oil-industry opposition to Ickes’s appointment and fears of permanent federal control.
subfiles.summary: Lawrence column on petroleum confusion and why Ickes was chosen, citing his NRA Oil Code experience; Ray Dudley fears federal coordination could become permanent control.

subfiles.title: No Sense to Gas Price Jump, Rideless Weekends
subfiles.about: Argues that the United States has abundant oil and that transportation, rather than supply, is the real problem.
subfiles.summary: Edson denies a physical petroleum shortage, citing restricted production, and surveys tankers, tank cars, trucks and pipelines to supply the seaboard.

subfiles.title: “Gas” for the Axis
subfiles.about: Demands an explanation for petroleum exports to Japan and Russia while Americans face fuel restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Letter 'Gas for the Axis' contrasts threatened gasoline restrictions with tanker transfers and exports to Japan and Russia, accusing the government and oil firms of aiding the Axis.

subfiles.title: Why the Tanker Diversion?
subfiles.about: Questions the diversion of fifty American tankers to British service and its effect on eastern petroleum supplies.
subfiles.summary: Editorial asks Ickes and the Maritime Commission to justify sending tankers to Britain amid eastern supply tightness, and whether lend-lease protects British commercial interests.

subfiles.title: Why the Tanker Diversion? (duplicate partial clipping)
subfiles.about: Reproduces most of the editorial questioning the transfer of American tankers to Britain.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate partial clipping: fifty diverted tankers could cause eastern shortages; calls for disclosure of Britain's tanker needs.

subfiles.title: Give the People the Facts
subfiles.about: Calls for a public explanation of domestic petroleum sacrifices alongside increased sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Editorial says Americans will accept gasless Sundays if the need is explained, contrasting Petroleum Institute warnings with Farish's announced added sales to Japan.

subfiles.title: For U.S. Fuel—For Japan
subfiles.about: Contrasts American gasless Sundays with unrestricted petroleum supplies for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cartoon 'For U.S. Fuel, For Japan': domestic motorists face restrictions while fuel flows to Japan.

subfiles.title: Doesn’t Mr. Public Realize an Emergency?
subfiles.about: Satirizes government demands for American gasoline restraint while exports continue to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cartoon: warnings of July shortage and restrictions contrast with gasoline flowing to Japan, blaming a public that is unaware of the emergency.

subfiles.title: Plug That Leak, Harold: How About Some Priorities Here?
subfiles.about: Urges Ickes to stop petroleum exports to Japan before restricting American motorists.
subfiles.summary: Editorial 'Plug That Leak, Harold' condemns continued petroleum sales after scrap controls, citing a sharp March export rise, and wants them halted before gasless Sundays.

subfiles.title: Give the People the Facts (continued or duplicate fragment)
subfiles.about: Repeats and extends the editorial argument that the public deserves an explanation of petroleum policy.
subfiles.summary: Fragment of 'Give the People the Facts': restrictions threatened at home while sales to Japan approved; the shortage is transportation, worsened by fifty tankers sent to Britain.

subfiles.title: The Customer Across the Pacific
subfiles.about: Shows Japan claiming exemption from proposed American gas and oil rationing.
subfiles.summary: Cartoon portrays an honorable Japanese customer getting American oil while the US considers rationing and gasless Sundays.

subfiles.title: Mr. Ickes’ Oil Shortage
subfiles.about: Blames tanker transfers and exports to Japan for the threatened American oil shortage.
subfiles.summary: Letter 'Mr. Ickes' Oil Shortage' criticizes warning citizens of shortages while Japan gets about 70,000 barrels a day, predicting more tanker transfers to Britain.

subfiles.title: Gas Rationing in Britain—Should Interest Mr. Ickes
subfiles.about: Uses Britain’s experience to warn that strict gasoline rationing could disrupt American defense production.
subfiles.summary: Editorial notes Britain restored private cars so workers could reach factories, and argues rigid American rationing could impair defense work.

subfiles.title: Appears to Be Writ Sarcastic
subfiles.about: Sarcastically requests a bicycle for visiting tankers loading petroleum for Japan at Richmond.
subfiles.summary: Letter asks where a bicycle can be rented for gasless Sundays to ride to Richmond and watch tankers load oil for Japan.

subfiles.title: Ickes Takes Control of Oil; Shipping to Be Major Problem
subfiles.about: Reports Roosevelt’s appointment of Ickes as petroleum coordinator and identifies transportation as the immediate supply problem.
subfiles.summary: Roosevelt directs Ickes to coordinate the American petroleum industry so military and civilian requirements can be met continuously and at reasonable prices. The report says crude supplies were adequate but diversion of tankers to aid Britain had created a distribution bottleneck, particularly on the Atlantic seaboard.

subfiles.title: Roll Out the Barrels—Softly
subfiles.about: Condemns secrecy surrounding large oil exports to Japan while Americans are warned to expect rationing.
subfiles.summary: Editorial 'Roll Out the Barrels' extrapolates from March 1941's 1,553,000 barrels, argues Japan is stockpiling for war, compares export secrecy to French trade with Germany, and appeals to Roosevelt.

subfiles.title: The Case for Continuing Limited Oil Shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Explains strategic arguments for continuing petroleum sales to Japan while reserving the option of cutting them if American needs require it.
subfiles.summary: Editorial admits public anger but argues limited oil shipments may keep Japan from the Dutch Indies and the European war, though cuts would be justified if defense needs demand.

subfiles.title: The Customer Across the Pacific (duplicate cartoon)
subfiles.about: Repeats the cartoon portraying Japan as exempt from American fuel rationing.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate cartoon again contrasts gasless Sundays in America with oil for an honorable customer across the Pacific.

subfiles.title: Vulnerability
subfiles.about: Warns that German long-range aviation and possible Atlantic bases make the United States vulnerable to attack.
subfiles.summary: Editorial 'Vulnerability' challenges the belief oceans protect America, citing Aviation on German bombers operating from distant bases, and concludes aid to Britain is essential.

subfiles.title: Are Ya Listenin’?
subfiles.about: Illustrates Göring’s claim that no island is unconquerable by naming vulnerable Atlantic and Caribbean islands.
subfiles.summary: Cartoon 'Are Ya Listenin'?' shows the Azores, Bermuda, Bahamas, Martinique and Cape Verde beneath Goering's declaration about islands, reflecting fears of Axis bases near the Americas.

subfiles.title: He Must Find New Means to Deliver the Oil
subfiles.about: Profiles Ickes and outlines his responsibilities as Petroleum Coordinator for National Defense.
subfiles.summary: Profile of Ickes's New Deal career and conflicts with industry, stressing the threatened shortage is a transport problem from tanker diversions and describing pipeline and tanker plans.

subfiles.title: Why Does the United States Go On Selling Oil to Japan?
subfiles.about: Questions the strategic logic and morality of continuing American petroleum exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Editorial: oil companies say they will stop exports when State directs; presents the fear an embargo would drive Japan to the Indies and asks if the US should show less resolve than the Dutch.

subfiles.title: Gasless Sundays
subfiles.about: Opposes domestic gasoline restrictions while an Axis partner continues receiving American oil.
subfiles.summary: Letter 'Gasless Sundays' supports aid to Britain but rejects restrictions that free petroleum for Japan, urging protest and stopping supplies to the Axis.

subfiles.title: More Facts on the Gasoline ‘Shortage’
subfiles.about: Uses British tanker statistics to question the diversion of American vessels and the resulting New England shortage.
subfiles.summary: Commentary quotes Wall Street Journal tanker figures suggesting Britain kept ample vessels, and says New Englanders deserve a government explanation.

subfiles.title: The Customer Across the Pacific
subfiles.about: Publishes the recurring cartoon contrasting American rationing with petroleum sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Tacoma Times reproduces the honorable-customer cartoon on its front page, showing Japan exempt from gasless Sundays.

subfiles.title: Japanese Ship Loads Oil Here as East Faces ‘Gasless Sundays’
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese freighters loading petroleum at Philadelphia and other eastern ports despite the tanker shortage.
subfiles.summary: Article: the Azuma Maru and other Japanese freighters load lubricating oil and gasoline near Philadelphia while eastern consumers face restrictions; discusses legal sub-aviation exports and American tankers under Panamanian registry.

subfiles.title: It’s About Time
subfiles.about: Welcomes Ickes’s intervention against a lubricating-oil shipment from Philadelphia to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Editorial calls sending 252,000 gallons of lubricating oil from the east coast incongruous amid rationing, urges action on Atlantic and Pacific exports, and proposes domestic oil reserves.

subfiles.title: Honest, Harold?
subfiles.about: Challenges Ickes’s call for domestic economy while large quantities of oil go to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cartoon 'Honest, Harold?': Ickes tells motorists to economize while oil wells feed '800,000 barrels a month for the Japanese war machine.'

subfiles.title: Japanese War Machine Running on U.S. Gasoline
subfiles.about: Depicts Japan’s war machine passing an America halted by a gasless Sunday.
subfiles.summary: Cartoon shows a Japanese military vehicle fueled by American gasoline while a sign reads 'Gasless Sunday.'

subfiles.title: Gasoline Shortage Just Another Foolish Bugaboo
subfiles.about: Denies that the United States faces a genuine gasoline shortage and questions the motives behind the warning.
subfiles.summary: Letter argues prorated oil fields could flood the market, suggests the scare serves prices or Ickes's control, and asks why gasoline still goes to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Gasless Sundays
subfiles.about: Discusses the social cost of Sunday motoring restrictions and distrust of Ickes.
subfiles.summary: The editorial says Americans would accept necessary conservation but objects that Ickes is an unpopular and authoritarian messenger. It contrasts 1941 automobile dependence with 1918 and argues that Sunday travel provides essential recreation and morale for workers, especially those laboring on defense projects.

subfiles.title: Gasless Sunday
subfiles.about: Proposes weekday automobile pooling as a less disruptive alternative to banning Sunday pleasure driving.
subfiles.summary: The editorial explains that automobiles had become necessities and that Sunday was the principal opportunity for family recreation. Accepting that eastern transportation shortages might require conservation, it suggests neighborhood weekday car pools rather than eliminating the family holiday.

subfiles.title: Japanese War Machine Running on U.S. Gasoline (duplicate cartoon)
subfiles.about: Repeats the cartoon contrasting Japanese use of American gasoline with a gasless Sunday at home.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate cartoon of Japan's war machine on US gasoline, stamped received by Interior June 18, 1941.

subfiles.title: A Visitor from Japan: Japanese Vessel Here to Load Oil
subfiles.about: Reports that the Azuma Maru would load 1,500 barrels of lubricating oil in Philadelphia under a government license.
subfiles.summary: Article: a Japanese vessel's oil apparently for Japan's air force in China; Laurence Hunter confirms the cargo licensed; compares threatened eastern curtailment and monthly Philadelphia loadings.

subfiles.title: Japanese Vessel Here to Load Oil (duplicate clipping)
subfiles.about: Duplicates the report on the Azuma Maru’s licensed loading of lubricating oil.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate clipping: the Japanese freighter takes 1,500 barrels at Pier 98 before New York and Japan; repeats consumption and tanker-reduction estimates.

subfiles.title: 800,000 Barrels of Oil a Month Going to Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph Driscoll, New York Herald Tribune
subfiles.about: Investigates the scale of American oil shipments to Japan and the administration’s hesitation to impose an embargo.
subfiles.summary: Driscoll reports over 800,000 barrels a month go to Japan while the east faces gasless Sundays; State fears provoking Japan toward the Indies; William Cole Jr. urges correction if shipments contribute to the tanker shortage.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese bunkering in the American republics
subfiles.about: Recommends an urgent response to Rio concerning petroleum sales to Japanese vessels.
subfiles.summary: Bonsal argues shortages make it undesirable to distribute petroleum in ways not supporting inter-American commerce or defense, linking the Rio telegram to bunkering Japanese vessels.

subfiles.title: Telegram 1026 concerning Japanese purchases at Brazilian ports
subfiles.about: Reports excessive Japanese purchases of petroleum products and lubricants in Brazilian ports.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 1026: Standard Oil says Japanese vessels at Brazilian ports buy petroleum far beyond shipboard needs and asks whether to refuse all supply or only excess.

subfiles.title: Instructions on petroleum sales to Japanese vessels in Brazil
subfiles.about: Directs American oil companies in Brazil to restrict Japanese purchases to necessary shipboard supplies.
subfiles.summary: Hull recommends limiting sales to estimated shipboard needs and requesting payment in dollars. The embassy may tell Brazil that Japanese overstocking is viewed unfavorably and could affect tanker allocations, pending establishment of a definitive American bunkering policy.

subfiles.title: Telegram 1025 on possible Brazilian requisition of oil
subfiles.about: Reports that the Brazilian Navy is examining whether to requisition the oil in question.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 1025: Caffery says the Brazilian Navy is considering requisitioning the petroleum in the related case.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on Japanese inquiries about Bolivian rubber
subfiles.about: Warns that Japanese representatives are seeking samples and information about Bolivian Yungas rubber.
subfiles.summary: British Embassy: Japan may seek Bolivian Yungas rubber by a route avoiding Brazilian export restrictions; quantities modest; suggests addressing it in Bolivia negotiations.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of British report on Bolivian rubber
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the warning about Japanese interest in Bolivian rubber and reports a request for investigation.
subfiles.summary: Finletter thanks the British correspondent for the July 18 letter; the La Paz Legation has been told to investigate.

subfiles.title: White House memorandum concerning Governor Olson’s telegram
subfiles.about: Requests that the State Department acknowledge Governor Olson’s telegram.
subfiles.summary: White House memo forwards Governor Olson's telegram, asking the Under Secretary to arrange a Presidential acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: Governor Olson’s telegram urging a complete embargo on Japan
subfiles.from: Culbert L. Olson, Governor of California
subfiles.about: Calls for an immediate, complete embargo on oil, petroleum products, and other war materials destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Olson says Californians oppose supplying Japanese aggression and urges denying oil or war cargo to the silk-laden Tatsuta Maru in San Francisco for its return voyage.

subfiles.title: Reply to Governor Olson on petroleum-export controls
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Olson’s embargo appeal and refers him to federal measures announced on August 1.
subfiles.summary: Hull conveys the President's appreciation for Olson's telegram and notes press accounts of the August 1 petroleum measures.

subfiles.title: Telegram on aviation gasoline stored at Dairen
subfiles.about: Reports the delivery of Japanese aviation gasoline to leased Standard Oil storage tanks at Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Chase: a third leased Standard Oil tank at Dairen is partly filled with aviation gasoline from a small Japanese tanker, with more drums arriving; copies to Tokyo, Beijing, Shenyang, Harbin, Chongqing and Shanghai.
